description: This dataset label groups several distinct vascular skin findings: cherry angioma (a benign capillary proliferation), angiokeratoma (a benign capillary ectasia with a rough surface, including a rare form associated with Fabry disease), pyogenic granuloma (a rapidly growing, benign capillary tumor that bleeds easily), and hemorrhage/hematoma (extravasated blood from trauma, not a tumor at all). These entities differ meaningfully in cause, growth pattern, and clinical significance.
taxonomy_note: VASC is a combined dataset category covering at least four clinically distinct findings. A prediction of 'VASC' does not indicate which specific vascular lesion is present, and the entities it covers range from entirely incidental (cherry angioma) to ones with a genuine bleeding risk and documented melanoma-mimicry (pyogenic granuloma, hematoma).
symptoms: Cherry angioma: firm red, blue, or purple papule, 0.1-1 cm, usually asymptomatic, may appear on the trunk
Angiokeratoma: asymptomatic blue-red papule with a rough or warty surface, usually under 5mm, does not resolve spontaneously
Pyogenic granuloma: painless red fleshy nodule, typically 5-10 mm, growing rapidly over a few weeks; surface may ulcerate, crust, or become verrucous
Hemorrhage/hematoma: a discolored area (reddish, purple, brown, or black depending on healing stage) from trauma, for example a subungual hemorrhage under a nail
warning_signs: Pyogenic granuloma bleeds easily or profusely with minor trauma and can recur after inadequate treatment; it shares many clinical and dermoscopic features with amelanotic melanoma, which is the most important differential diagnosis
Cherry angioma and angiokeratoma may be confused with nodular basal cell carcinoma or amelanotic melanoma, which is why diagnostic removal is sometimes performed

Subungual hemorrhage: a normal-appearing proximal nail as it grows out excludes a melanocytic cause; irregular pigmentation across the full nail length, irregularly spaced pigmented bands, pigment extending onto surrounding skin (Hutchinson sign), or nail dystrophy/ulceration are melanoma warning signs
Hematomas can be dermoscopically indistinguishable from acral lentiginous melanoma in some cases; without a clear trauma history, biopsy or excision may be needed to exclude melanoma
recommendation: Cherry angioma and angiokeratoma generally do not require treatment. Pyogenic granuloma and any lesion without a clear trauma history, or with atypical/melanoma-like features, warrant dermatologist evaluation, and biopsy or excision may be used specifically to exclude melanoma.
